----------------------------------------------------------------
EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN
----------------------------------------------------------------

1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with staggered adoption, complemented by an event-study specification.  
Why appropriate:  
• Treatment (program roll-out) varies across both counties and years, generating panel variation well-suited for DID.  
• The evaluation question is average causal impact on treated counties relative to the counterfactual evolution of similar but untreated counties—exactly what DID is designed to capture.  
• An event-study (relative-time coefficients) reveals dynamic effects and allows a formal visual/pre-trend test.  
• Recent advances (Callaway-Sant’Anna 2021, Sun-Abraham 2021) correct for heterogeneous treatment effects, avoiding bias in two-way fixed-effects (TWFE).

2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable:  Treat_{ct}=1 from the first year county c becomes eligible for / starts receiving the specific local economic development program; 0 beforehand. After initiation, treatment is assumed to be absorbing (stays at 1).  
Control group: All counties that never receive the program during the sample period (“never-treated”), plus the not-yet-treated counties in years prior to their adoption (“not-yet”).  
Treatment timing: For each treated county c, Event Time = Year t – first_treatment_year_c.  
RDD not used; no running variable required.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1. Parallel trends: In absence of the program, treated and control counties would have followed similar outcome paths.  
⋯ Plausibility: Programs were often allocated based on past economic distress, but conditional on county fixed effects, state–year fixed effects, and flexible controls (lagged outcomes, population, industry mix), residual trends are plausibly parallel.  
A2. No differential anticipation: Households/firms do not significantly change behavior before formal program start. Short pre-treatment windows help test this.  
A3. Stable unit treatment value (no cross-county spillovers): One county’s program does not materially affect outcomes in control counties. This is more plausible if programs are geographically targeted and commuting zones are controlled for.  
A4. Treatment adoption is conditionally exogenous after controls (e.g., not driven by unobserved shocks coinciding with county-specific booms).  
A5. No composition changes: county boundaries/population measurement stable.

4. Main Threats & Mitigation  
T1. Economically distressed counties self-select into programs → violates parallel trends.  
   • Include county fixed effects, state×year fixed effects, county-specific linear trends, and pre-trend tests.  
   • Propensity-score or synthetic-control re-weighting (Callaway-Sant’Anna) to improve covariate balance.  
T2. Heterogeneous treatment timing bias in TWFE.  
   • Use Sun-Abraham or Callaway-Sant’Anna estimators instead of vanilla TWFE.  
T3. Spillovers to neighboring counties (e.g., job seekers commute).  
   • Add spatial lags as controls; drop counties within 50 miles of treated counties as robustness; or re-define treatment at the commuting-zone level.

5. R Code Outline

```r
# 0. Packages
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)           # fast high-dim FE
library(did)              # Callaway-Sant’Anna
library(lmtest); library(sandwich)

# 1. Load data
df <- read_csv("county_panel_1960_2009.csv")

# 2. Variable construction
df <- df %>% 
  mutate(treat_first_year = ifelse(Treatment==1, year, NA)) %>%
  group_by(county_fips) %>%
  mutate(first_treat_year = min(treat_first_year, na.rm = TRUE),
         ever_treated    = ifelse(is.finite(first_treat_year),1,0),
         rel_time        = year - first_treat_year) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(rel_time = ifelse(!ever_treated, NA, rel_time),
         post = ifelse(year >= first_treat_year & ever_treated==1, 1, 0))

# 3. Main TWFE specification (for reference; report but do not rely on)
twfe <- feols(outcome ~ post | county_fips + state_year, data = df, cluster = ~county_fips)

# 4. Sun-Abraham event-study (in fixest >=0.10)
es_sa <- feols(outcome ~ sunab(first_treat_year, year) | county_fips + state_year,
               data = df, cluster = ~county_fips)

# 5. Callaway-Sant’Anna ATT
cs <- att_gt(yname = "outcome",
             tname = "year",
             idname = "county_fips",
             gname = "first_treat_year",
             xformla = ~ pop + unemployment_rate_lag + median_age,
             data = df)
agg_cs <- aggte(cs, type = "group")  # overall ATT

# 6. Robustness check: drop border counties within 50 miles
border <- read_csv("county_borders.csv")       # pre-computed adjacency matrix
df_rb <- df %>% filter(border_to_treated==0)
cs_rb <- att_gt(yname = "outcome", tname = "year",
                idname="county_fips", gname="first_treat_year",
                data=df_rb)
```

6. Expected Results  
Economic theory (agglomeration economies, multiplier effects) suggests positive impacts. I expect:  
• Employment rate +1.5 – 3 percentage points within five years post-treatment.  
• Real per-capita income +4 – 6 percent cumulatively after a decade.  
Heterogeneity: larger effects in counties with initially higher human-capital stocks; negligible or even negative spillovers on neighboring untreated counties.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (for DID)  
C1: No differential pre-trends → 0.8 (needs to be tested)  
C2: Correctly modeled treatment timing / absorbing state → 1  
C3: No interference between units → 0.5 (possible spillovers)  
C4: No other simultaneous policy shocks → 0.7 (state-year FE mitigate)  
C5: Consistent outcome measurement across counties/years → 1  

Average score ≈ 0.8 → identification reasonably credible, with spillovers and pre-trend equivalence the main caveats.
